pitch_detail.notes: Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows to Surprise Lake / Warm Lake, ~8-9 mi one way.
Ridge travel mixing snow and loose rock, Gilbert visible most of the way.
Snow travel/glacier crossing on the southeast side, crampons recommended.
Short, loose scramble through a notch to the true summit; no significant exposure on most lines but rock is unstable.

emergency.notes: Cell coverage is unreliable near trailheads and throughout the wilderness; this is the more remote of Gilbert Peak's routes.
emergency.rangerStation: Cowlitz Valley Ranger District, Gifford Pinchot NF — (360) 497-1103, 10024 US Hwy 12, Randle, WA 98377

before.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack; this is a glacier-approach mountaineering line — carry an ice axe, crampons, and consider a rope for glacier travel on Conrad Glacier.
before.pro_needs: Basic glacier travel kit (axe, crampons) for the Conrad Glacier crossing to the saddle, then boulder/scree/snowfield travel to the summit (Mazamas).

before.beta: From a base camp at Snowgrass Flats, climbers cross south toward the Old Snowy/Ives Peak massif and traverse a series of rock ribs and shallow gullies (the 'Goat Ledges' and 'Goat Ribs') at roughly 7,400-7,600 ft toward Gilbert Peak. The key navigational feature is a band of solid, abrasive white pyroclastic aggregate that points toward a notch behind a prominent dark rock tower nicknamed the 'black prow'; staying on this band (rather than the looser rock above or below it) is described as the safest line. A lower variation holds a consistent ~7,500 ft traverse elevation to reduce exposure to party-induced rockfall. The route is regarded by some as loose and dangerous, but careful route-finding along the white band and goat paths allows a safer class 4 passage to the summit.
before.approach: Drive to the Berry Patch or Snowgrass Flat Trailhead (Chambers Lake area) off Forest Road 21/2150 on the west side of the Goat Rocks: turn east onto FR 21, continue about 13 miles, turn at the Snowgrass Trail/Chambers Lake sign onto FR 2150, then follow signs to the Snowgrass Flat Trailhead (elev. ~4,650 ft). Hike Trail #96 (Snowgrass) roughly 4 miles and ~2,000 ft of gain along Goat Creek to Snowgrass Flats, a large subalpine meadow used as base camp; from there head cross-country/scramble east across the Goat Ledges/Goat Ribs traverse toward Gilbert Peak (often combined with Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak in one traverse day).

approach_variants.name: Snowgrass Flats and the Goat Ledges traverse to the black prow
approach_variants.notes:
Drive to the Berry Patch or Snowgrass Flat trailhead in the Chambers Lake area on the west side of the Goat Rocks, at about 4,650 ft, reached by forest road off the highway west of Packwood. Hike Snowgrass Trail #96 roughly 4 miles and about 2,000 ft along Goat Creek to Snowgrass Flats, a large subalpine meadow used as base camp.

From camp, head cross-country and scramble east across the Goat Ledges and Goat Ribs — a series of rock ribs and shallow gullies — at roughly 7,400-7,600 ft toward Gilbert Peak. This is often combined with Old Snowy and Ives in a single traverse day.

A lower variation holds a consistent traverse elevation of about 7,500 ft, which reduces exposure to rockfall knocked down by other parties.

The route is regarded by some as loose and dangerous. Careful route-finding along the correct band and on goat paths is what makes it a reasonable class 4 passage rather than a bad one.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the ledges are dry
hazards: Significant rockfall on the Goat Ribs and Goat Ledges traverse, worst with parties stacked at different elevations
Loose andesite, pyroclastic breccia and tuff throughout the upper mountain
Steep, insecure sections approaching the summit block even in dry late-season conditions
Route-finding failure — the whole route depends on correctly identifying the white aggregate band
A class 4 downclimb through the notch on the way back, on the same loose ground
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE WHITE BAND IS THE ROUTE. THAT IS THE ENTIRE FINDING AND IT IS A COLOUR TEST, WHICH IS WHY IT SURVIVES BAD LIGHT.

On the Goat Ribs and Goat Ledges traverse at roughly 7,400-7,600 ft there is a band of SOLID, ABRASIVE, WHITE PYROCLASTIC AGGREGATE. It points at a NOTCH BEHIND A PROMINENT DARK ROCK TOWER — the black prow. So there are two objects to find and they are opposite colours: a white band and a dark tower, with the notch behind the tower.

THE NEGATIVE IS TACTILE AND IT TELLS YOU IMMEDIATELY, WITHOUT A VIEW: THE WHITE BAND IS SOLID AND ABRASIVE. THE ROCK ABOVE IT AND BELOW IT IS LOOSE. If the holds are moving under your hands you are off the band — traverse back to the white rather than pressing on.

HOLD YOUR HEIGHT AT ABOUT 7,500 FT. Drifting HIGH is worse than drifting low: it puts you above the band and above other parties, in the position that generates the rockfall this traverse is notorious for. The low variation is a deliberate choice, not a mistake.

THE BASE OF THE CLIMBING IS THE NOTCH BEHIND THE BLACK PROW. Everything before it is traversing; the class 4 finish begins there. If you are scrambling steeply and you have not passed a dark tower, you have started up too early.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: the traverse ends at the peak. If the ribs and gullies keep coming and you have not found a white band pointing anywhere, you are on the wrong tier of the mountain — go back to a rib you can identify and re-find the band, rather than gaining height to look.

timing.recommendedStart: Early morning start from Snowgrass Flats camp to allow a full day for the Old Snowy/Ives/Gilbert traverse

what_to_bring: Extra water (creeks can run dry by late summer)
Backpacking/camping gear for a Snowgrass Flats base camp
before.descent: Reverse the Goat Ledges/Goat Ribs traverse and white-aggregate-band route back to Snowgrass Flats camp, then hike out Trail #96.
before.itinerary: Commonly done as a multi-summit traverse from a Snowgrass Flats camp: Day 1, hike in to Snowgrass Flats (or Lower Snowgrass); Day 2, traverse to and climb Old Snowy Mountain, Ives Peak, and Gilbert Peak in a single long day (reported round-trip totals of ~22 miles and ~7,500 ft cumulative gain/loss for the full multi-peak traverse) before returning to camp; Day 3, hike out.
